tldr: On a miniature 270 g quadruped robot with endless 360-degree rotation and no joint limits, upright walking, inverted walking, and landing recovery are unified into a single RL policy that runs entirely onboard a microcontroller.
hero_caption: The onboard data path running at 50 Hz. The upper microcontroller (ESP32-S3) handles observation creation and inference of the small neural network, while the lower microcontroller (ESP32-C3) bridges communication between the IMU and servomotors, achieving fully autonomous control with no offboard PC required.
overview:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has become common for locomotion control in medium and large quadrupeds. However, at the sub-kilogram miniature scale, severe computational constraints and large sim-to-real gaps have kept fully onboard, closed-loop learned locomotion out of reach.

The authors tackle this challenge with "MiNI-Q," an ultra-lightweight 270 g quadruped whose 8 joints are belt-driven and capable of continuous rotation without mechanical stops. Because the legs can rotate fully, the robot can flip upside down and continue walking simply by rotating its legs. Exploiting this geometric symmetry, the authors introduce continuous joint posture commands on the torus $T^8 = (S^1)^8$ and gravity-conditioned transformations. This unifies upright walking, inverted walking, and landing recovery into a single, compact neural network without any finite state machines or mode switching.

To transfer this policy to the physical robot, they carried out actuator identification on a single-leg testbed, cross-engine validation across simulators, and an embedded inference pipeline accelerated by SIMD instructions on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller. Furthermore, domain randomization of foot geometry allows the robot to handle previously unseen foot attachments without retraining.

Hardware experiments showed stable forward velocity tracking in both upright and inverted walking, immediate recovery to walking in 24 out of 30 drop-release trials, and robust locomotion across four interchangeable foot geometries on four indoor surfaces.
contributions: Leveraging mechanical symmetry with no joint limits to unify upright walking, inverted walking, and landing recovery into a single learned policy without state machines.
Achieving unified, continuous posture and tilt transitions during locomotion via angular embeddings on the torus space and gravity conditioning.
Demonstrating 50 Hz closed-loop control on 270 g hardware using a dual-microcontroller setup with servo identification and SIMD-optimized inference, eliminating the need for an offboard PC.
Showing zero-shot transfer to unseen physical foot shapes and various indoor floor surfaces through foot-geometry domain randomization.

sections.heading: Can a 270 g palm-sized robot keep walking even when flipped upside down?
sections.summary: Achieving fully onboard, closed-loop learned locomotion on sub-kilogram miniature quadrupeds has been extremely difficult. Using MiNI-Q with its continuous-rotation legs, this work successfully unifies upright walking, inverted walking, and landing recovery into a single policy running directly on microcontrollers.
sections.details:
In recent years, reinforcement learning has dramatically boosted the dynamic performance of quadruped robots. Yet for sub-kilogram robots weighing under 1 kg, most deployments still rely on replaying precomputed trajectories or offloading computation to an offboard PC. At this scale, motor backlash, extremely light links weighing only about 1 g causing numerical integration breakdown in simulators, and tight microcontroller memory and compute budgets present severe barriers.

This study focuses on "MiNI-Q," a palm-sized quadruped weighing just 270 g. Its defining feature is that all 8 joints are belt-driven with no mechanical rotation limits (no joint stops). Consequently, the range of motion for each joint is the circle $S^1$, making the full joint space an 8-dimensional torus $T^8 = (S^1)^8$. Thanks to this mechanism, even if the body flips upside down, the robot can form supporting ground configurations simply by sweeping its legs 180 degrees.

The crucial design choice here is avoiding the traditional state-machine approach, where a fall triggers a dedicated get-up controller. Instead, the authors exploit mechanical symmetry to express upright walking, inverted walking, and landing recovery within a single policy. By applying an algebraic transformation that flips the target posture depending on the gravity vector's direction, they achieve seamless transitions with no control mode switching.

sections.heading: Where does this fit in miniature robotics and unified locomotion?
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work on miniature quadruped robots and recent RL methods for diverse locomotion under a single policy. The key uniqueness of this study is exploiting continuous-rotation joint geometry to realize fully onboard, unified control without relying on external computers.
sections.details:
### Miniature Platforms and Embedded Learned Control
While research on small quadrupeds like Petoi Bittle and Stanford Pupper is active, deploying learned controllers on physical hardware has generally required single-board computers like a Raspberry Pi or wireless communication with an offboard PC. Microcontroller-only inference exists in niche domains like nano-drones, but closed-loop control running entirely on microcontrollers in sub-kilogram quadrupeds is exceptionally rare. This work achieves it using an energy-efficient dual-microcontroller setup.

### Locomotion Learning and Sim-to-Real Transfer
Combining massively parallel simulation tools like Isaac Gym with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) has sped up quadruped locomotion training by orders of magnitude. For larger platforms (such as ANYmal and Unitree), transfer to hardware is well established through detailed actuator modeling and domain randomization. Building on these standard pipelines, this paper adapts them to an ultra-lightweight robot using precise servomotor system identification and foot-geometry randomization.

### Conditioned Behaviors and Posture Control
Approaches like "Walk These Ways" have popularized conditioning a single neural network to execute diverse walking styles, postures, and gaits. However, previous platforms all operated with bounded joint limits. This study differs fundamentally by prescribing postures continuously over the joint space $T^8$ and leveraging continuous rotation to capture inverted locomotion under the exact same framework.

sections.heading: How do torus geometry and gravity flipping connect the behaviors?
sections.summary: The authors introduce a periodic embedding $(\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$ to remove wrap-around discontinuities, alongside a target posture inversion map conditioned on the gravity vector's sign. Coordinated posture interpolation and drop curricula then train stable walking and recovery together.
sections.details:
### III-A Task and Command Space
Commands to the policy consist of forward velocity, yaw rate, and an 8-dimensional joint posture target $\theta^p$. The policy—a compact MLP with under 25k parameters—outputs joint position offsets relative to the reference posture, which are sent to actuators at 50 Hz. The exact same network runs continuously during drops, impacts, and steady walking.

### III-B Posture Conditioning and Inversion Symmetry
To anchor posture commands, the authors define seven reference anchors (Figure F2): three baseline gaits (Crouch, ANYmal-like, and Q8bot-like) and four tilted variations (Nose-up, Nose-down, Lean-left, Lean-right). Because joint angles wrap around on the circle $S^1$ at $2\pi$, geodesic interpolation using the shortest angular difference enables continuous intermediate postures rather than just discrete anchors.

Furthermore, when the robot flips upside down (indicated by a sign change in the projected gravity vector $g_z$), the policy applies an algebraic leg symmetry map: $\mathcal{I}(a,b) = (\pi - a, -b)$. This switches the target posture to its inverted counterpart, equivalent to rolling the hardware 180 degrees. As a result, upright and inverted locomotion share a single command interface without any finite state machine (FSM).

### III-C Periodic Observations and Policy I/O
Feeding raw joint angles $\theta$ into the policy introduces steep discontinuities at the $\pm\pi$ wrap-around boundary, disrupting training. To resolve this, angles are projected onto a 2D plane via the Whitney-type periodic embedding $E(\theta) = (\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$, providing a smooth representation on $T^8$. In addition, because physical joint velocity sensors are noisy, they are omitted from the observation. Instead, a 3-frame history of joint offsets and projected gravity vectors is provided, allowing the network to infer velocities implicitly.

### III-D Recovery and Posture Curricula
To ensure stable learning, posture and drop curricula are expanded concurrently (Table I). Training begins around single anchors, advances to interpolation between nearby anchors, and finally spans distant anchors. The drop curriculum similarly progresses from upright drops to lateral orientations, and ultimately to free falls from up to 0.5 m with full 3D rotations in $\mathrm{SO}(3)$.

### III-E Foot-Geometry Domain Randomization
Physical 3D-printed feet change shape over time due to wear or component replacement. To build tolerance against these variations without retraining, each simulation environment is randomly assigned a sphere (radius 7.5 mm) or one of three cylinder profiles with varying lengths, along with contact distance offsets.

sections.heading: How is the microcontroller inference pipeline built and calibrated?
sections.summary: A dual-microcontroller setup (ESP32-S3 and ESP32-C3) runs closed-loop control at 50 Hz without external communication. Detailed actuator identification on a single-leg testbed overcomes the control challenges unique to ultra-lightweight robots.
sections.details:
### IV-A Platform and Control Interface
MiNI-Q weighs 270 g, with individual leg links weighing only about 1 g. It uses Dynamixel XL330-M077-T miniature servos, driving two degrees of freedom per leg via timing belts. The servos operate strictly in position control mode. The high-level policy sends position targets at 50 Hz, and internal PD loops drive the motors.

### IV-B Actuator Identification via Hardware Calibration
In ultra-lightweight link mechanisms, gear friction and armature (rotor) inertia inside the motor dominate the dynamics. The authors mounted a single leg on a calibration testbed (Figure F7, left) and gathered experimental data using step responses and sinusoidal sweeps. By optimizing stiffness, damping, rotor inertia, and friction parameters in MuJoCo using the Nelder-Mead simplex method, tracking error (RMSE) was reduced by a factor of 17 to 20 (from 0.49 rad down to approximately 0.027 rad) compared to nominal PD models.

### IV-C Embedded Implementation (Onboard Inference)
Onboard computation is handled by an ESP32-S3 dual-core microcontroller. Core 0 executes policy inference as a high-priority FreeRTOS task, while Core 1 manages I2C communication with the secondary microcontroller (ESP32-C3). By utilizing the ESP32-S3's 128-bit SIMD instructions (PIE128) for matrix multiplications and storing weights in DRAM, single inference latency dropped to just ~594 microseconds. This accounts for only ~3% of the 50 Hz (20 ms) control loop budget, leaving ample headroom for real-time execution.

captions.F7: Actuator identification setup. Left: Single-leg testbed. Right: Measured hardware response (red) versus the nominal PD model (orange), which drifts significantly, and the identified model (blue), which matches the physical behavior with high precision.

sections.heading: What were the training configurations and real-world benchmarks?
sections.summary: Training completed in roughly 8 hours on a single RTX 4090 across 4096 parallel Isaac Gym environments. Physical experiments used an external tracking camera strictly for evaluation while testing posture changes, landing recovery, and foot swaps.
sections.details:
### V-A Training Setup
The policy was trained with PPO across 4096 parallel environments in Isaac Gym, using a 2 ms physics step and a 50 Hz (20 ms) policy update rate. During training, the critic network received 22 dimensions of privileged information unavailable on hardware—such as base linear velocity, disturbance forces, and uncorrupted joint velocities—while the deployable actor network received only onboard-accessible observations. Training ran for 20k iterations and completed in roughly 8 hours on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.

### V-B Hardware Setup and Evaluation Protocols
Hardware experiments evaluated a single learned checkpoint without any fine-tuning or mode switching. An external ZED2 camera and AprilTags recorded ground-truth trajectories, but this visual data was used solely for evaluation logging and never fed into the robot's control loop. Testing covered four common indoor surfaces—MDF, polycarbonate, artificial turf, and rubber sheeting—spanning static friction coefficients between 0.3 and 0.7.

sections.heading: Did it work on real hardware? Locomotion, recovery, and foot generalization
sections.summary: The physical robot achieved stable velocity tracking in both upright and inverted postures (RMSE 0.037 m/s and 0.050 m/s). It also demonstrated dynamic posture transitions while walking, an 80% recovery success rate from drops, and zero-shot adaptation to unseen foot attachments.
sections.details:
### VI-A Velocity Tracking in Upright and Inverted Locomotion
Velocity tracking tests were conducted on hardware in both upright and inverted configurations (Figure F4). For a target velocity of 0.15 m/s, forward velocity RMSE was 0.037 m/s upright and 0.050 m/s inverted. Locomotion quality remained comparable after flipping upside down, all while running the exact same policy. Because the 2-DOF legs lack abduction/adduction (hip roll) joints, initiating turns requires large sweeping leg motions to overcome static friction, which introduces slight initial oscillations in yaw rate tracking before converging smoothly to the target.

### VI-B Continuous Posture Transitions during Locomotion
In a 25-second continuous hardware run at 0.15 m/s forward speed, target anchors were sequenced through ANYmal, Nose-down, Nose-up, Crouch, and Q8bot postures (Figure F5). As the torus distance $d_{T^8}$ transitioned in steps, the robot smoothly modified its body height and pitch while maintaining steady forward walking.

### VI-C Landing Recovery from Free Falls
The robot was dropped or tossed from heights of 20 to 30 cm across various orientations to see if it could resume commanded walking within 5 seconds of touchdown. As shown in Table III, it succeeded in 24 out of 30 trials (80% success rate) across upright pitch/roll, inverted pitch/roll, and toss conditions (6 trials each). All 6 failures stemmed from hardware limits under impact—servo over-current shutdowns (torque-off), loose battery terminal connections, and belt teeth slipping—rather than policy breakdown.

### VI-D Adaptation to Interchangeable Feet
Three physical foot shapes not seen during training (Hexagonal, Square, and Spike; Figure F6, left) were 3D-printed and tested across four indoor surfaces. The robot maintained upright walking across all 16 foot-surface combinations without falling. The highest tracking error occurred with the spike foot on artificial turf (RMSE 0.136 m/s), where spikes snagged on carpet fibers, but on rigid surfaces RMSE remained below 0.08 m/s.

### VI-E Simulation Ablations
Ablation experiments in simulation confirmed the necessity of each component (Table VI). Removing the gravity-conditioned inversion map caused inverted tracking performance to drop from 1.00 down to 0.02. Removing periodic embeddings and feeding raw angles reduced performance to 0.21. Omitting the drop curriculum lengthened average recovery time from 6.9 s to 9.7 s.

captions.F5: In-flight posture transition experiment. While tracking forward velocity, target postures transition (ANYmal -> Nose-down -> Nose-up -> Crouch -> Q8bot). Joint state ($d_{T^8}$) tracks continuously while forward walking continues uninterrupted.

sections.heading: What does this achieve, and what hardware limits remain?
sections.summary: While continuous-rotation legs proved highly effective for unified locomotion, the experiments also highlighted hardware challenges unique to miniature robots, including servo impact tolerance, backlash, and lateral drift due to missing hip degrees of freedom.
sections.details:
The key breakthrough of this work is mathematically formalizing continuous rotation as an unconstrained geometric degree of freedom. This blurs the line between recovery behaviors and normal walking, pushing the dynamic envelope of ultra-lightweight robots.

At the same time, clear limitations remain. Velocity tracking error was around 25% to 33% relative to the commanded speed (0.15 m/s), which is less accurate than larger quadrupeds. Because the legs lack hip abduction/adduction joints, turning requires forcing the feet to slide against floor friction through large sagittal strokes, making lateral drift hard to avoid.

Additionally, all drop recovery failures were caused by electrical or mechanical impact issues. Landing impacts from 20 to 30 cm caused Dynamixel servos to trip over-current protection, momentarily disconnected power terminals, or skipped belt teeth. This highlights an important takeaway: no matter how robust the recovery policy is, physical shock absorption remains a hardware bottleneck.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A new paradigm expanding behavioral repertoires in miniature robots
sections.summary: This study demonstrated unified upright walking, inverted walking, and drop recovery on a 270 g continuous-rotation quadruped using a single policy running fully onboard. Leveraging mechanical symmetry through geometric formulation opens practical avenues for miniature robot autonomy.
sections.details:
In this paper, upright walking, inverted walking, landing recovery, dynamic in-flight posture morphing, and foot shape generalization were unified into a single neural network with roughly 25k parameters on the 270 g continuous-rotation quadruped MiNI-Q.

Executing 50 Hz closed-loop control on an onboard dual-microcontroller system (ESP32-S3 + ESP32-C3) without external compute or wireless communication represents an important milestone for sub-kilogram robotics. By translating the physical trait of continuous rotation into mathematical tools (torus geometry and gravity inversion), the authors unlocked remarkably versatile, robust behaviors without adding control complexity.

Future work includes autonomous selection of optimal postures based on tasks and terrain, as well as multi-robot cooperative tasks involving swarms of miniature quadrupeds.

sections.heading: Appendix: Periodic embedding geometry and cross-engine validation
sections.summary: This appendix covers the mathematical foundation for bounded distortion in periodic embeddings, the composition of the 22-dimensional privileged critic, and cross-engine debugging that prevented simulator integration breakdown.
sections.details:
### Bounded Distortion of Periodic Embeddings
For an angle $\theta \in S^1$, mapping to $(\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$ means that for any geodesic distance $\delta \in [0, \pi]$ between two points, the Euclidean chord distance in the embedded space $\mathbb{R}^2$ is $2\sin(\delta/2)$. Elementary geometry yields $(2/\pi)\delta \le 2\sin(\delta/2) \le \delta$. Extending this to all 8 joints guarantees that the map from $T^8$ to $\mathbb{R}^{16}$ has upper- and lower-bounded metric distortion, providing a smooth, easily learnable input space for the neural network (Figure F9).

### Breakdown of the 22-Dimensional Privileged Critic
To stabilize training, the critic network received privileged observations withheld from the actor: base linear velocity (3D), base height above terrain (1D), random disturbance forces and torques (3+3 = 6D), uncorrupted joint velocities from simulation (8D), and an environment-specific base mass scaling factor (4D). The deployable actor policy relies solely on clean, reliable onboard sensor signals.

### Pitfalls in Simulator Numerical Integration
During early development, simulating ~1 g links under torque control (effort mode) with 2 ms time steps in Isaac Gym led to severe simulation blowups due to stiff contact solver iterations. The team diagnosed this by mirroring identical model parameters in MuJoCo (1 ms torque control) and Isaac Lab to cross-check observation pipelines and dynamic behaviors. Consequently, they adopted position-control mode in Isaac Gym, matching the position-command interface used on the physical hardware.

takeaways: Removing mechanical joint stops enables continuous rotation, creating a strong morphological advantage that eliminates mode switching for inverted walking and landing recovery.
Combining periodic embeddings $(\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$ with gravity-conditioned symmetry maps naturally unifies upright and inverted locomotion under a single RL policy.
SIMD vector instructions and DRAM memory placement are crucial for microcontroller inference, allowing an ESP32-class chip to execute a 2-layer MLP in well under 1 ms.
For miniature robots with link masses of just a few grams, identifying internal motor friction and rotor inertia, as well as tuning contact integration steps, determines sim-to-real success.
limitations: Lacking hip roll (abduction/adduction) actuators forces turns to rely on aggressive leg sweeping against ground friction, resulting in initial yaw oscillations and noticeable lateral drift.
All landing recovery failures were caused by physical hardware limits under shock, such as servo over-current shutdowns and timing belt tooth slippage.
Hardware testing was conducted primarily on a single unit over flat indoor surfaces, leaving unit-to-unit hardware variance, rough terrain, and outdoor environments for future validation.
